Surgical Breast Enlargement

Who Is a Candidate for Breast Reduction?

Breast reduction removes breast tissue and skin to reduce size and weight. It is often done for physical symptoms as well as appearance.

Home/Surgical Breast Enlargement/Breast reduction/Who Is a Candidate for Breast Reduction?

Breast reduction removes breast tissue and skin to reduce size and weight. It is often done for physical symptoms as well as appearance. See Breast Reduction.

Symptoms that often lead people to consider it

  • Neck, shoulder or back pain
  • Deep grooves from bra straps
  • Skin irritation or rashes under the breasts
  • Difficulty exercising or finding clothes that fit
  • Poor posture
  • Headaches or numbness in the hands
  • Distress about breast size

These can have other causes, so a doctor should check for them.

What the surgeon assesses

  • Breast size, weight and shape
  • Skin quality and nipple position
  • Your general health and weight
  • Breast screening history and family history
  • Your goals and expectations

Factors that favour surgery

  • Breasts that have finished developing
  • A relatively stable weight
  • Good general health
  • Realistic expectations
  • A non-smoking status

Factors that need discussion

  • Smoking, which affects healing
  • Plans for pregnancy or breastfeeding
  • Obesity or medical conditions
  • Plans for significant weight loss, which may change breast size

Non-surgical steps first

Supportive bras, physiotherapy and weight management may help some people. Surgeons may suggest these first, especially when symptoms are mild.

Document symptoms and their effect

Keep a simple record of pain, rashes, strap grooves, activity limits and treatments you have tried. This helps a clinician look for other causes and understand how breast size affects daily life. It is useful information, but it does not replace examination or guarantee that surgery is the right answer.

Goals are more than a cup size

Cup sizes differ between brands and do not describe breast width, shape, scars or nipple position. Explain which activities or clothing are difficult and what amount of change feels acceptable. A surgeon can discuss a range of likely proportions, but cannot promise an exact bra size.

Screening and timing

Tell the surgeon about previous lumps, biopsies, implants, family history and any screening that is due. Significant weight change or pregnancy plans can alter breast size and shape, so timing may matter. A review can help decide whether waiting would make the result more predictable.

Questions to ask

  • Am I suitable now, or should I wait?
  • How much reduction is realistic?
  • What would you do if I plan pregnancy?

Key takeaway

Suitability depends on health, symptoms and goals, not size alone.
